evidence.label: Elementary positivity of chromatic quasisymmetric functions
Lean scope doc
evidence.note: The scope doc says the formalization proves elementary positivity over ℕ[q] and links 1 Comparator challenge.

headline: A coloring count with an extra q-weight always splits into elementary pieces with nonnegative coefficients.
scope: The result covers every natural unit interval graph, a family of graphs built from overlapping runs of consecutive vertices. It does not address the companion unimodality conjecture.
plain: Count the ways to color a graph so that linked vertices differ. Weight each coloring by q raised to its number of rising edges. Shareshian and Wachs conjectured that, for natural unit interval graphs, this weighted count splits into elementary pieces with never-negative whole-number coefficients. This paper proves it, with each coefficient counting an explicit set of permutations.
doesNot: This does not prove the elementary unimodality part of the Shareshian–Wachs conjecture.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Richard Stanley and John Stembridge, the q = 1 conjecture
scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles the positivity part of a well-known refined conjecture, and gives each coefficient a counting meaning.

explanation:
Take three vertices in a row, labeled 1, 2 and 3, with links 1–2 and 2–3. Color each vertex red, green or blue, so linked vertices never match. Such a coloring is called proper, and there are 12 of them. Rank the colors red < green < blue.

Now tag each coloring by its rising edges. An edge rises when its lower-numbered vertex gets the lower color. Coloring 1, 2, 3 red, green, blue makes both edges rise. Blue, green, red makes neither rise. The other ten colorings each have exactly one rising edge. Give each coloring the weight q raised to its number of rising edges. The 12 weights add up to 1 + 10q + q².

Allow any number of colors, and keep track of which colors are used. The result is the chromatic quasisymmetric function of the graph. With q set to 1, it is Stanley's chromatic symmetric function from 1995, which refines the usual count of colorings[9].

Formulas like this can be rewritten in elementary pieces. The piece e_k adds up all products of k different color variables. For the three-vertex path, the paper's expansion is q·e₂e₁ + (1 + q + q²)·e₃[3]. Check it with three colors. Then e₂e₁ counts 3 × 3 = 9 and e₃ counts 1. So the total is 9q + 1 + q + q², which is the 1 + 10q + q² found above. Every coefficient here is a polynomial in q with nonnegative whole-number coefficients. That property is called elementary positivity over ℕ[q].

Shareshian and Wachs proved that this function is symmetric for natural unit interval graphs[2]. In such a graph, vertex i links to a run of the next few vertices, and these runs never shrink as i grows. They conjectured that every such graph is elementary-positive over ℕ[q][2]. The q = 1 version is the older Stanley–Stembridge conjecture from 1993[10]. Hikita proved that q = 1 version in 2024. His formula gives positive values for every positive real q, but not whole-number coefficients[12]. Griffin, Mellit, Romero, Weigl and Wen gave an independent proof of the q = 1 version[13]. Earlier formulas did not give a nonnegative coefficient for each separate elementary piece[14].

This paper proves the refined conjecture for every natural unit interval graph[1]. It also says what each coefficient counts. Take permutations of the vertex labels where any drop between neighbors in the list is a linked pair. Weight each by q raised to its number of out-of-order linked pairs[4]. A step-by-step procedure then sends each such permutation to one elementary piece. For the three-vertex path, the permitted lists are 123, 132, 213 and 321, with weights 1, q, q and q². One of the two q lists goes to e₂e₁ and the other three go to e₃[5]. Setting q to 1 recovers the Stanley–Stembridge theorem[11].

The single hard part is subtraction. Counting colorings gives nonnegative numbers, but rewriting in elementary pieces can introduce minus signs[8]. The paper first matches each coefficient with an algebraic object known to be positive. It then turns those algebraic identities into explicit one-to-one matchings of finite sets[15]. The procedure always finishes, but its running time may be large[7]. The paper makes no claim about unimodality, the second half of the conjecture[6].

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked a formal version of the elementary expansion over ℕ[q]. It covers every finite number of color variables, with each permutation weighted as above. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major. Lean checks a formal version of the elementary expansion over ℕ[q]. The paper leaves the unimodality part open, and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A way to give each vertex a color so that no two linked vertices share one.
A graph on vertices 1 to n where each vertex links to a run of the next few vertices, and these runs never shrink as you move right.
A formula that lists every proper coloring and tags it with q raised to its number of rising edges.
The sum of all products of k different variables, written e_k.
Writable as a sum of products of elementary symmetric functions, using only coefficients that are never negative.
Polynomials in q whose coefficients are whole numbers 0, 1, 2 and so on.

claims.sourceQuote: This proves the elementary-positivity part of the Shareshian--Wachs conjecture.

claims.sourceLine: Shareshian and Wachs proved that this function is symmetric for this graph
claims.sourceQuote: Shareshian and Wachs proved that this function is symmetric for this graph class and conjectured that its coefficients in the elementary basis belong to $\N[q]$ \cite{SW16}.

claims.text: For the path 1–2–3 the expansion is q e_(2,1) + (1+q+q²) e_(3); colorings with a repeated color give q m_(2,1) and the rest (1+4q+q²) m_(1,1,1).
claims.sourceLine: To check this directly, the colorings with a repeated color contribute
claims.sourceQuote: To check this directly, the colorings with a repeated color contribute $q\,m_{(2,1)}(X)$, while those with three distinct colors contribute $(1+4q+q^2)m_{(1,1,1)}(X)$.

claims.text: Each coefficient counts permutations with no forbidden descents, weighted by q to the number of inversions on edges.
claims.sourceLine: counts only inversions supported on edges
claims.sourceQuote: Thus $D_G^0$ forbids adjacent descents between nonneighbors, and $\ginv_G$ counts only inversions supported on edges.

claims.text: For the path, the theorem assigns one degree-one permutation to (2,1) and the other three permutations to (3).

claims.sourceQuote: The theorem assigns one of the two degree-one permutations to $(2,1)$ and the other three permutations to $(3)$.

claims.sourceQuote: His formula gives numerical nonnegativity for every positive real $q$, while its rational $q$-weights do not establish coefficientwise nonnegativity in $\N[q]$; the refined conjecture remains explicitly distinguished in \cite[Section~1.3]{Hik24}.
